title: Angry Anderson, who soundtracked Kylie Monigue's wedding in Neighbours scene, dies aged 79
description: Rock star Angry Anderson, whose music famously soundtracked the wedding of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan's characters in Australian TV soap Neighbou
body: Rock star Angry Anderson, whose music famously soundtracked the wedding of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan's characters in Australian TV soap Neighbours, has died at the age of 79.The musician, whose real name was Gary Anderson, rose to fame as the frontman of Rose Tattoo, one of Australia's most revered rock bands, from 1976.His solo song Suddenly became a global hit after it was played during the wedding of Minogue and Donovan's characters Scott and Charlene in Neighbours. The episode was watched by 20 million people in the UK in 1988.Anderson said Minogue had been "adamant" that the track was used for the scene, and he later declared that Suddenly was the best song he had ever written.Paying tribute to Anderson on Instagram, Donovan said: "Legend! What a great guy."Another great Australian. Thank you Angry for all the wonderful music and memories. Condolences to all friends and family."Before his death, Anderson had a cardiac arrest while on Rose Tattoo's farewell tour in Europe last month.He was treated in hospital before going home to Australia, and the band cancelled nine live dates.A joint statement, external from Anderson's family and Rose Tattoo remembered him as a "devoted father, and much-loved bandmate"."His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas," it said."We thank everyone for their prayers and messages of love and continued support."Born in Melbourne in 1947, Anderson and Rose Tattoo first became known on Australia's rock scene, releasing five albums beginning with their 1978 debut.After the band split nine years later, Anderson continued recording music as a solo artist, and co-wrote and released Suddenly in the summer of 1987.It was quickly selected by Minogue for use in Neighbours for her character Charlene Mitchell's wedding to Donovan's Scott Robinson.Thanks in large part to its use in Neighbours, Suddenly reached the top three in both the UK and Australia.However, it was held off the number one spot in its home country by Minogue's own debut solo single, Locomotion.Anderson released two albums as a solo artist, before Rose Tattoo reunited in 1993 to support Guns N' Roses on their Australian tour.The band returned in 1998 for their own tour and were inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) Hall of Fame in 2006.Anderson's other credits included playing Herod in an Australian production of Jesus Christ Superstar.He was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 1993, in recognition of service to the community, particularly his charity work and his work as a youth advocate.

schema.headline: Angry Anderson, who soundtracked Kylie Monigue's wedding in Neighbours scene, dies aged 79

title: Azerbaijan frees jailed Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
description: French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges
body: French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list. Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine". The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive".  Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative". French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China."I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

schema.headline: Azerbaijan frees jailed Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire

title: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
description: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's ho
body: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead."Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

schema.headline: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

title: Salva Kiir: South Sudan president dissolves government ahead of country's first elections
description: South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in
body: South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in 2011.The country has previously postponed elections twice and extended the transitional period several times.Under the amended law, signed on Monday, Kiir removed the country's five vice-presidents and dissolved parliament, as well as national and state governments.Kiir is the presidential candidate of his Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM).  No prominent figures have announced plans to challenge him in the December poll. The main opposition leader Riek Machar was sacked as vice-president last year and charged with treason.He is under house arrest.Machar had been named vice-president as part of a 2018 peace deal to end a five-year civil war between forces loyal to the two men.Kiir will remain in office with full constitutional powers until an elected president is sworn in. He also reappointed some ministers and governors in caretaker positions until the 22 December elections.Ahead of Tuesday's announcement a heavy security presence was reported in the capital, Juba. Soldiers from the army and national security services blocked access to government ministries. Soldiers were also seen patrolling parts of the city.A senior government official told the BBC that staff arriving for work were turned away and told to return the following Monday. UN agencies in Juba also asked staff to work remotely while the situation was monitored.Kiir last week dismissed the chairman of the national elections commission, Abednego Akok Kacuol, without giving a reason. He was replaced by the commission's secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng. Akok had said in August that the commission needed $250m (£190m) to conduct the election but had received only $21m.In June, the main opposition group, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO), the party of Machar, warned people not to take part in poll preparations."Anyone coming to register voters and campaign in territories controlled by the mighty SPLM-IO, you will be a prisoner of war," Nathaniel Pierino, acting chairperson of the group, said in a post on Facebook.The body which oversees implementation of the 2018 peace agreement, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC), said South Sudan had entered a "critical phase".It said several key talks under the agreement remained incomplete and urged the parties to agree on a path towards credible elections and a peaceful end to the transitional period, which has lasted since independence.The latest 24-month extension was due to end on 22 February 2027.

schema.headline: Salva Kiir: South Sudan president dissolves government ahead of country's first elections

title: Nigeria prison deaths: Inside the cell where 33 inmates lost their lives
description: Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.The day before he had bee
body: Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m  (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation."I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin. The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window."One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door.  That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe."People were calling for help, some were already very weak."But no-one came to help, he and others allege."While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency."We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door."We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye."The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.

schema.headline: Nigeria prison deaths: Inside the cell where 33 inmates lost their lives

title: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban
description: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.Gunmen stormed a house in the K
body: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".While the motive of the shooting has not yet been confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings". "Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects, who were said to be carrying pistols and rifles.South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.Although South Africa has long had a high murder rate, mass shootings are a more recent problem and elicit increased feelings of unsafety, fear and shock. The phenomenon has led to calls for the government and law enforcement authorities to do more to dismantle organised crime networks and, in some cases, "murder for hire" syndicates – believed to be among the leading instigators of the attacks. Much has also been said about improving the economic conditions that make crime an attractive enterprise for some. There are no easy answers for how to solve South Africa's crime problem but security experts believe that the high proliferation of illegal guns, insufficient visible policing in high crime spots, the slow pace of justice and allegations that senior politicians and police officers have links to criminal gangs all add to the pervasive sentiment that local authorities are losing the fight against crime.

schema.headline: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban

title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
description: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's lega
body: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people."Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said."A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's  security detail for the last 20 years of her life.Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police."All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August. Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death."She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement."Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation

title: Hurricane Polo downgraded but remains 'very powerful' off coast of Mexico
description: Figure caption, Did El Niño turn Hurricane Polo into the most powerful storm of the season?ByBrandon LivesayUpdated 1 hour agoHurricane Polo, a large
body: Figure caption, Did El Niño turn Hurricane Polo into the most powerful storm of the season?ByBrandon LivesayUpdated 1 hour agoHurricane Polo, a large storm off the coast of Mexico, has been downgraded to category 4 but remains "very powerful", the US National Hurricane Center said.The Pacific hurricane, one of the strongest of the season, was projected to head towards the coast of south-western Mexico, bringing intense wind and rain, though was not expected to make landfall. A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts.The slow-moving storm is being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon.It was previously a category 5 storm - the highest level on the scale - but was downgraded to category 4 on Wednesday morning. Forecasters said that the storm was expected to fluctuate in intensity over the next few days. Image source, CSU/CIRA & NOAA/Handout via REUTERSAs it slowly drifts north west, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast, and "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the forecaster said. Forecasters said heavy rainfall associated with Polo could impact coastal regions in southwest Mexico through Thursday. A tropical storm warning remains in effect for portions of southwest Mexico and a tropical storm watch is in effect west of Playa Perula, the National Hurricane Center said.The hurricane centre said people under a tropical storm warning should expect conditions to develop on Wednesday, and those in the watch areas can expect conditions to develop by Thursday.Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days."So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk. So far this season, the Pacific has seen 15 storms, all in early September. Polo is the strongest of a batch of three storms currently swirling between Hawaii and the North American mainland.Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Members of the National Guard patrol a beach as Mexico prepares for Hurricane PoloScientists monitoring the ocean temperatures say the current El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record.Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds.El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.

schema.headline: Hurricane Polo downgraded but remains 'very powerful' off coast of Mexico

title: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says
description: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrend
body: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.Nato is thought to have several thousand troops stationed in the Baltic state, including US and German forces. Although the US is currently reviewing its deployments in Europe, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday that a new US troop rotation was on its way to his country.Sinkevičius told the BBC. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly.""We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year, which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally.Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons.The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons.Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops in Lithuania, but says now that it is unable to give a precise figure for the numbers stationed there.Germany - a fellow Nato ally - has pledged to send a 5,000-strong combat-ready brigade to Lithuania permanently as a response to the changing security situation in Europe. However, Nato said on Tuesday it would reach "full operational capability"  by the end of 2027.The Germany military has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions.The majority of troops will be based in Rūdninkai, near the Suwałki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad.The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus.UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace."We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."Moscow did not comment on the incident.Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members".

schema.headline: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says

title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
description: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a seri
body: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA).One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says, external the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence".It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN.Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis, external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed.Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressingOne displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says.Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023.Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17."The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system".While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire.Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety.Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable.One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15."Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is."The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women."We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad."The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining.The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war.The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike.Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point.""If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home."A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain."Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms.The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers. This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%.Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war."One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report.Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes.There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer.If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available in the UK at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds

title: White House rolling out red carpet for historic Xi Jinping visit
description: Figure caption, Watch: What’s at stake when Trump and Xi meet in the US?ByBrandon DrenonReporting fromWashington DC Updated 4 hours agoUS President Do
body: Figure caption, Watch: What’s at stake when Trump and Xi meet in the US?ByBrandon DrenonReporting fromWashington DC Updated 4 hours agoUS President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Washington, with AI, trade and Taiwan expected to be on the agenda for the leaders of the global superpowers. Xi will be greeted personally by Trump at Andrews Air Force Base on the eve of a White House state dinner and a military flyover.The three-day trip marks Xi's first state visit to the US since 2015 and his third meeting with Trump in the past year. Adding to the high-stakes state visit, a US-China trade agreement reached last year is set to expire in November.The trade truce - reached in October 2025 as Trump and Xi met in South Korea - saw Washington suspend steep tariff increases on Chinese goods while Beijing eased back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing.Experts said they will be watching for some sort of announcement around an extension of this agreement during the forthcoming state visit. Xi's trip to Washington, which ends on Friday, will have plenty of pomp and pageantry, and includes lavish dinners, private tours and performances.He will be accompanied by First Lady Peng Liyuan who is expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with US First Lady Melania Trump on Thursday.Figure caption, Watch: Rare look at the remote data centres powering China's AI ambitionsDavid Sacks, a fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the planned extravagant welcome by Trump as "really unprecedented".  "From meeting Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base to having a flyover for Xi as well, this is not something afforded to any US ally," Sacks said, "much less an adversary like China."It's quite, quite stunning," he continued.Trump is expected to address several issues as he meets Xi, particularly on tariffs and trade. The US president has long criticised his country's trade deficit with China, which stands at more than $91bn (£68.2bn), according to the latest US Census Bureau data, external. Also, Chinese rare earth exports to the US are down, external despite the agreement last October. US and Chinese officials held trade talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, but failed to make meaningful progress ahead of the Xi visit, multiple sources told the BBC.The talks focused on finding areas of agreement around non-tariff trade issues and agricultural exports, according to sources familiar with White House thinking. US negotiators were expected to continue talks with Chinese counterparts in Washington on Wednesday after Xi's arrival.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, China's First Lady Peng LiyuanAnother likely talking point between Trump and Xi is artificial intelligence, a topic that David Firestein from the Bush China Foundation said has "climbed rapidly toward the top of the agenda" ahead of this visit.China and the US are competing in what has been described as an AI arms race. But after a series of recent high-profile security incidents involving the emergent technology, there has been growing pressure on the Trump administration to regulate AI and slow its development. Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X this week: "For the sake of all humanity, Trump and Xi must negotiate a treaty NOW to pause AI and ban superintelligence before it's too late." Trump's former White House adviser Steve Bannon and some Republicans in Congress have also warned about dangers posed by AI. The president, who views the technology as vital to the US economy and a battleground in a global struggle for power, has been reluctant. He views defeating China in the AI race as a primary objective. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump has said. Firestein told the BBC he expects Trump and Xi to discuss ways for AI collaboration.On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, and said the two had "very successful" talks on trade and AI.Several AI and tech industry titans will attend a White House state dinner on Thursday, according to US officials. Open AI's CEO Sam Altman, Jensen Huang, whose company Nvidia makes chips that power AI, and X boss Elon Musk are some of the dinner attendees.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Open AI CEO Sam Altman at the White House in September 2025Experts who spoke to the BBC said any major breakthroughs on AI or other issues are unlikely to occur during the Trump-Xi meetings this week.Then there is Taiwan, which remains a diplomatic thorn. The US Congress has approved a multibillion-dollar arms sale to Taiwan that awaits Trump's signature. He has held off for now, viewing the move as a bargaining chip with China.Beijing has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan and has not ruled out the use of force.Firestein said he expects Xi will be looking for Trump to either commit to extending the delay of the arms sale or somehow avoiding the sale altogether. Xi - like Trump - is also facing economic headwinds at home, and is expected to use this visit to discuss deepening US-China trade. However, that presents a potential political problem for Trump. Some members of his cabinet and his supporters view China with deep suspicion. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a letter, external to Ford Motor Company in September, urging the company to cut ties with China due to national security concerns and protection of American jobs. Regardless of the clear hurdles that remain before any new US-China deals are inked, it is clear that Trump views personal contact with Xi as vital to the process."Trump has made a decision that no matter what, we need to not have a confrontational relationship with China," Stephen Orlins, president at the National Committee on US-China Relations, said."He believes that the more he and President Xi meet, the less confrontational that relationship will be," Orlins continued, "and he is right."With additional reporting by Daniel Bush, Washington correspondent

schema.headline: White House rolling out red carpet for historic Xi Jinping visit

title: Morocco election: How Ceuta, football and Israel have shaped the campaign
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballotByBasma El AttiDisillusioned young
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballotByBasma El AttiDisillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality."I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Some 60,000 people swam from Morocco to the Spanish territory of Ceuta in late JulyHamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda."As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history."We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031."As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."Image source, Fifa via Getty ImagesImage caption, Morocco's FA president Fouzi Lekjaa is beloved by fans for helping put the Atlas Lions on the world football stageFouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise."The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Huge pro-Palestinian protests often take place in RabatAlso seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on  a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations."We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh."If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".Siham AzeroualI think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24."I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot."Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach."I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.You may also be interested in:

schema.headline: Morocco election: How Ceuta, football and Israel have shaped the campaign

title: Israel vs Republic of Ireland - how Uefa Nations League matches became so contentious
description: An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.That the ma
body: An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest. In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide"."We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".

schema.headline: Israel vs Republic of Ireland - how Uefa Nations League matches became so contentious

title: OpenAI gives AI cyber defence tools to Ukraine
description: The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure,
body: The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks.According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025.Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes.Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable.George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services."Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014. "Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said.Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict. "Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said.He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country.But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google.The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack.Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation. Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models.The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York. AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering. United Nations Secretary General António Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence".Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine. It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm.Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services.Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks.But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face. Anthropic, and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents.Additional reporting by Chris Vallance

schema.headline: OpenAI gives AI cyber defence tools to Ukraine

title: Trump media ban: Administration accuses outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
description: According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting inciden
body: According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation. It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting."Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."Ahead of Wednesday's hearing, 49 media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - filed a legal brief in support of the lawsuit against the White House.  Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.On Tuesday, tensions continued between Trump and some of the news outlets, as Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlin Collins before his speech to the United Nations General Assembly: "I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me."Collins noted later on air that the network had made no such pledge.He also took to social media to attack Collins, once again asking why she and others were reporting on the president at the UN. The US president also hit out again at CNN , Politico and MS NOW, calling them "treasonous".

schema.headline: Trump media ban: Administration accuses outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
